query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature sliding conditions, the FeNiCrCoCu coating dynamically forms an ultra‐nanocrystalline, oxidized surface layer that activates a twin‐assisted deformation pathway (via an inverse Hall–Petch effect) and thereby governs the overall wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating with a relatively coarse, metastable microstructure and minimal preexisting oxide scale.
generation.intervention: Expose the coating to controlled high-temperature sliding wear (e.g., 700–800°C) compared to a baseline test at lower temperature or without a pre‐oxidation treatment.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests under high-temperature operating regime (approximately 700–800°C) in an environment that permits in situ oxidation (e.g., ambient air or controlled oxygen partial pressure).
generation.structural_mediator: A dynamically formed, ultra-nanocrystalline tribolayer that is enriched in oxides.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures under sliding contact, shear stress and heat promote dynamic recrystallization and surface oxidation. This leads to the formation of an ultra-fine (nanocrystalline) and oxidized near-surface layer. The refined grain size enables increased deformation twinning, which, coupled with the protective nature of the oxide scale, enhances wear resistance via an inverse Hall-Petch mechanism.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, the high-temperature treatment will result in lower wear rates, reduced friction coefficients, and a microstructure in the worn surface that shows increased twin density and a nanocrystalline oxide-rich layer.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited coating (or low-temperature sliding test) that exhibits a coarser grain structure, lower twin activity, and higher wear rates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in the high-temperature regime (700–800°C) where dynamic oxidation and recrystallization are activated; at lower temperatures, the same microstructural transformation may not occur.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative interplay between oxide layer thickness, degree of grain refinement, and the extent of twin activation remains uncertain, as does the precise effect of slight compositional variations on these mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical FeNiCrCoCu coatings and subject them to sliding wear tests at both high temperature (700–800°C) and a control low temperature. Use TEM/SEM to analyze the worn surface for the presence and characteristics (grain size, twin density, oxide composition) of a nanocrystalline tribolayer. Simultaneously, measure wear rates and friction coefficients.
measurements: Surface grain size and twin density (via TEM/SEM)
Oxide layer thickness and phase composition (via XPS or EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-temperature sliding tests do not yield a significant ultra-nanocrystalline, oxide-rich layer with increased twin activity—i.e., if microstructural analysis shows no refinement or if wear rates and friction coefficients do not decrease compared to the baseline—the hypothesis is falsified.

Microstructure and Mechanical Properties Evolution of the Al, C-Containing CoCrFeNiMn-Type High-Entropy Alloy during Cold Rolling

Abstract: The effect of cold rolling on the microstructure and mechanical properties of an Al- and C-containing CoCrFeNiMn-type high-entropy alloy was reported. The alloy with a chemical composition (at %) of (20–23) Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni; 8.82 Mn; 3.37 Al; and 0.69 C was produced by self-propagating high-temperature synthesis with subsequent induction. In the initial as-cast condition the alloy had an face centered cubic single-phase coarse-grained structure. Microstructure evolution was mostly associated with either planar dislocation glide at relatively low deformation during rolling (up to 20%) or deformation twinning and shear banding at higher strain. After 80% reduction, a heavily deformed twinned/subgrained structure was observed. A comparison with the equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy revealed higher dislocation density at all stages of cold rolling and later onset of deformation twinning that was attributed to a stacking fault energy increase in the program alloy; this assumption was confirmed by calculations. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2).
